www.fastretailing.com/eng/about/company/profile_yanai-koji.html so the film gives some nod to the fact that there's discontent within this worker despite his happy veneer throughout everything else that had transpired until that point. but does it explain what this could be or how it could come to happen? there is some interpersonal drama and we witness some cheating, but there is little if any attention paid to the structure these things exist in. when his coworker disappears and a new person shows up the next day, this just happens. the higher ups have taken care of it. and no further questions are asked. in [this one interview] yakusho says that his character sees the homeless man in the intersection and is moved by that he's the only one to really do so; but does he? this is a caricature too! and the film dupes us because we're grafted onto him. we have no choice in the operation, and it's made sure of that every step of the way. the whole thing is choreographed form the very beginning. take the tic-tac-to game, for example; there you have yakusho initially thinking it's just trash. the audience at this point is like, no! what are you doing, don't you see there's greater value there!! but then he realizes his mistake and even plays along. and this becomes a subplot of the film, of him filling out the tic-tac-to game, playing against some yet unseen opponent. and then when the game is over, he gets a thank you note for his role as such. and we get satisfaction in this because he did what we wanted him to. the film shines light on his face when his coworker's (ex?)girlfriend suddenly kisses him, but don't worry, it's just the light of the car door suddenly opening, no secondary function here. (by which i mean to say that this is specifically queuing us to receive this scene in a certain way). we get led along the whole time and then at the end there this pretense that it was all worth it but that life's tough and you just have to keep on. but what the real final shot is, it need be understood, gives the actual game away. that is, the grand city scape and the shining sun. while i'm not anti-city or anything like this, it's necessary to understand the relation to city that this film has from the point of its very inception. this is literally a propaganda piece for The Tokyo Toilet initiative -- an "urban revitalization" (we can just say gentrification, you don't have to be so coy) program masterminded by Yanai Koji, son of Uniqlo's CEO Yanai Tadashi. we can get another glimpse of this in a chance scene that happens when Yakusho comes across an older man standing in front of a developing plot. The old man asks Yakusho if he remembers what used to be here. Yakusho doesn't answer and the old man concludes, that's what it means to get old (you forget what used to be). But this is literally not true! Or, it doesn't have to be. It is not an inevitability of life that high end toilets financed by plastic industry and fast fashion will displace the perfectly functioning ones that existed before. It's not the fault of the people for forgetting, it's that there's a literal ongoing violence that makes people forget. And then part of this too can be the whole system of atomization that this is all tied up in, where people just exist as individual subjects, maybe tending to their own idiosyncratic archive, but there is no collective knowledge share -- there is no means of coming together and producing a history of what things have been like so that this knowledge can be passed down to future generations. Instead you get family heirlooms and hand-me-downs. Everything is purely familial, the film wants us to believe. Which has problems because generational wealth doesn't exist! This shit is stolen goods. And then so what, it's just too bad for people that never got a foothold to begin with? There has to be a better way. Perfect Days grew out of an institutional advertising campaign linked to The Tokyo Toilet, a project to redesign public toilets in Shibuya. An invisible class cleans these designer spaces so Tokyo can preserve its image as a polished, sophisticated metropolis. The film seems to make one of those workers visible, yet aestheticises his invisibility and romanticises his life: the toilets barely get dirty, his body shows no wear and his pay or insecurity remain off-screen. The job becomes ritual and spiritual fantasy. Wenders does not dignify cleaning; he reshapes it to fit his own idea of beauty

El monótono y rutinario trabajo de un limpiador de baños en Tokio, con una vida aburrida y rutinaria en un entorno aburrido y rutinario día tras día hasta la llegada de una visita Sigo sorprendido unos días después de como una historia absolutamente ABURRIDA tiene comentarios que la consideran algo notable en el cine de los últimos años. Dos horas de la vida de un señor que limpia baños públicos en Tokio, amanece, trabaja, baño, come, lee y vuelta a empezar salvo un trozo tras HORA Y CUARTO DE LO MISMO donde aparece la sobrina y medio entiendes algo de todo esto. Sinceramente y con todo el respeto me gustaría saber a qué se debe tanto halago a una película donde su guion no es nada, solo destaca la actuación del protagonista y tirar de éxitos musicales de los 70. ¿Qué nos quiere decir Wenders? Debes ser feliz desde una vida rutinaria y monótona, sino pues te jodes. Cinematográficamente la película tiene un par de cositas buenas: -	Protagonista despierta simpatía + ambigüedad en su pasado. -	La fotografía está elaborada y cuidada. El mensaje se podría haber resumido en 15 minutos, como mucho podría ser un corto. Parece una coña pero la película surge cuando el Tokio Toilet Project invitó a Wim Wenders a la capital para que observara los aseos públicos que habían diseñado famosos arquitectos en Shibuya. Wenders está prendado de Japón y su mundo desde hace décadas e interesado en la arquitectura del país. Dear Wim Wenders, I've tried, man. I really tried with this one. Your films, while esthetically pleasing, carry nothing in terms of substance, story, or attention. I'm not saying I need action packed, narrative expository, tiktok noise to keep me invested, but Jesus Christ, Wim, give me something to work with. Your films are flat. They engage with the lonely side of life and less about the slice of it - and that's something to be commended for. But not everyone is lonely. Not everyone feels that way. And sometimes a lonely day is not that engaging. If I wanted to see a lonely slice of life piece that's a little more engaging, I would rather just watch a documentary. I'm sorry Wim, but I feel you will never write anything that's neither engaging or worth my time. The closest you got to making a film that explores loneliness while keeping your audience somewhat entertained was 42 years ago and it definitely shows. Maybe you're a lonely man who wants everyone else to feel as lonely as you, and maybe that's the point of your films. But I don't to feel that way everytime I want to engage with your art. You'll never change and that's okay, but I don't think I'll invest in your talent ever again. Your fans are few but dedicated, and your quality speaks to them in ways that I will never comprehend. I'm sorry I can never be part of that dedicated community that sees the beauty of your world, and I'm sorry I can't see what you see. Maybe someday I might, but not banking on that anymore. But keep making your art anyway. Film as a whole needs voices like yours. Sincerely, A.F.X. Heller

From the beginning to the midpoint, Perfect Days beautifully captures the life of a lonely working-class man in Japan, living a quiet, repetitive, and seemingly monotonous routine. The arrival of Niko briefly disrupts that routine, revealing a different side of Hirayama and adding a welcome sense of warmth to his otherwise solitary life. The soundtrack is easily the movie’s strongest aspect. Every song comes from the ’60s to the ‘80s, and for me, it’s a perfect 10/10. Each track complements its scene beautifully. The sequence featuring “Sunny Afternoon” by The Kinks instantly reminded me of The Boat That Rocked, which also used the song to great effect. Despite its simplicity, the movie contains several memorable visual moments. One of my favorites is the zoom-out shot as Hirayama walks into the bookstore. It’s subtle, but it perfectly matches the movie’s calm, contemplative atmosphere. To me, the movie reflects the contrast between the peaceful life many people dream of and the emotional exhaustion that can come from living the same routine every single day. Sometimes, all you can do is force a smile just to keep yourself going. That said, despite its meaningful message about quietly enduring life’s hardships, I felt the movie sacrificed too much in favor of symbolism. The story is rather underdeveloped, there aren’t many scenes that stayed with me, and too much is left implied without strengthening Hirayama character enough for me to form a deeper emotional connection. Music: 10/10 Movie: 5/10

Great cinematography, but I'm so sorry; the story is boring af. How tf am I supposed to watch someone's GRWM for 10 consecutive days? Don't get me wrong—I absolutely get what Wim Wenders is going for here. After watching this, I genuinely appreciate sanitation workers more. I also found myself paying more attention to the little details of everyday life. In that sense, the film absolutely succeeds. But that's also where it stopped for me. Like Mr Hirayama, I'm an introvert. But as far as I long to know myself, I'd still go out and socialise. I can imagine how exhausting his routine must be—waking up before sunrise, cleaning toilets all across Tokyo, dealing with strangers who can be kind one minute and awful the next. So it makes perfect sense that he spends the rest of the day rewarding himself with some introvert treats of 'me time'. But he has a coworker, and despite the contrast personality, Mr Hirayama chose not to say a single word. EVERY SINGLE DAY!! Ikr, deep inside, Mr Hirayama is a genuinely kind person. You can barely look at how he carefully handles his loving plants and cherishes nature. He's just painfully reserved. That said, I never felt emotionally invited into his inner world. Maybe I'm a judgmental person, so I spent most of the time observing him rather than truly understanding him. If the story had offered a little more variety or a stronger narrative hook, I probably would've loved it despite our contrasting personalities, just like his coworker to him. But as it stands, this is one of those films I admire far more than I actually enjoy. It's Wim Wenders, after all. A fun ride was probably never the point.

C’est parce que le protagoniste est transfuge, parce qu’il a un certain capital culturel, une certaine sensibilité à la vie bonne qu’il fait autant d’effort pour être heureux (parce que c’est un effort de trouver entre les moment de travaux de beaux moment) c’est parce qu’il subit pas la précarité qu’il peut se permettre ce retrait. Ça reste désastreux et encore plus qu’on pourrait imaginer : le projet vient de Koji Yanai, dirigeant de Fast Retailing (Uniqlo), qui cherchait à faire connaître ces toilettes à l’international et voulait un documentaire signé par un grand réalisateur, c’est une commande de communication autour d’un projet d’architecture financé par une multinationale du textile, transformée en méditation sur la dignité. Demorei quase uma semana pra começar a escrever sobre esse filme, isso porque as sensações eram bem mistas e ele realmente me fez refletir sobre diversos temas. Eu gosto de como o filme começa, gosto de como a rotina ritualística de Hirayama é, apesar de repetitiva, diferente todos os dias por meio do que é ignorado, gosto da cadência com que ele nos é apresentado: aos poucos, enquanto nós só observamos sem compromisso, acompanhando a vida do protagonista sem de fato saber quem ele é. Entendo a posição contemplativa que Wenders tenta nos colocar, a de olhar através dos olhos do protagonista ou da lente de sua câmera. Creio que esse seja o principal ponto onde o longa pode ou não funcionar, a depender da capacidade individual de um espectador de enxergar beleza nessas pequenas coisas (o que não é nem um pouco fácil) e é também onde, pelo menos pra mim, Wenders fracassa em transmitir esse valor, chegando a soar artificial em certos momentos, pois o filme no fim das contas ainda é uma encomenda publicitária, e porque extrai sua beleza do que já é belo, não do que é banal e visto como tal. Não acho que o filme seja fetichista ou romantize um trabalho como o de limpador de banheiros, tampouco ingênuo em afirmar que tudo são flores e que problemas não existem, eles existem. Acredito que a escolha de não mostrar o impacto do preconceito ou do cansaço no protagonista pode ser interpretada como parte justamente da filosofia dele, e a forma como ele vive, mas até que ponto? A partir da segunda metade do filme, o usso e abuso da principal característica e filosofia de vida do personagem (resiliência estoica, contemplação, serenidade e deslocamento/distância) como justificativa para a falta de dramatização e proximidade expulsa a trama dos próprios trilhos. Parece que o filme frequentemente nos carrega pra uma situação dramática com grande peso para ele, mas sempre que algo precisa de tempo para ser sentido, até mesmo tempo para que haja a dúvida de por que um limpador de banheiros escolheria deliberadamente a vida que tem, o filme foge e inicia um novo dia, com a mesma desculpa. Tenho fé que deve existir alguém que nem o Hirayama por aí, mas que esse alguém É ou em algum momento foi/será maluco, eu tenho é certeza.

I solemnly swear that I am not being a contrarian by rating this low. On a technical level, this is not a bad film by any means. The cinematography is gorgeous, with very nice shot composition. I admired the crisp, tactile sound design. I liked the editing and thought the performances were solid. Everything else just didn’t do it for me, and I don’t think I’d recommend watching this film to anyone. I don’t wish to yuck anyone’s yum, but the level of praise this gets from people baffles me. A previous version of me would deride those people, but I now know better not to stoop to that. At the very least, I get why others appreciate it so much, I just can’t see the appeal in a way where I’m in the appreciator crowd, if that makes sense. Barely anything happens in this movie. You watch the protagonist go through the same loop: his work schedule, his hobbies, his habits, etc. There are minor deviations along the way that shake things up, but nothing intensely interesting, nor anything that really moves a strong narrative forward, with the exception of his niece showing up later in the film. Before you tell me I “missed the point”, I know for certain that I recognized the point of the film, I suppose I just don’t accept it. Maybe I don’t necessarily reject the point outright, I just don’t like the execution. It's two hours long, for the general message of appreciating life. For me, that’d be fine for a short film, but two hours just for that?! Watch a video about the importance of being present, then meditate for five minutes. You’ll get more value that way. “But, PolynesianSpa,” you say. “That’s the point. The fact that you cannot bear a two hour film about living in the moment shows that you are impatient and restless. You missed the point, for you do not appreciate the little things, you do not relish simplicity, nor do you revel in mundanity. You are incongruent with the essence of the film.” you lecture. Touché. I don’t jive with this movie on a personal level, that’s just not who I am. Still, usually I can enjoy things that I don’t directly relate to, if I like the execution enough. This just felt like a massive waste of time. Perhaps it was a lesson. I’ll admit it. I’m envious of the film’s protagonist. Hirayama lives a life of mediocrity, but that doesn’t seem to bother him. As a toilet cleaner, he is technically a vital part of the upkeep of civilization, yet I imagine it is a thankless job that does not pay as much as it should. Regardless, he does not stew in dissatisfaction. He makes the absolute most of what he has. Not me. I’ve been stuck in a slightly-above-minimum-wage job for too long. What exasperates my frustration with the film is that I myself don’t have even the slightest amount of dedication that Hirayama has. He has this unrelenting commitment to routine and work, despite said routine and work not really yielding much fulfillment. I am also of the belief, especially in our age of hypercapitalist exploitation, that one shouldn’t bust their ass for a boss/company that doesn’t care for them at all. Do your job and do it right, but don’t wear yourself out for the sake of the corporate fat cats who own you. Hirayama lacks revulsion for his overlords, choosing instead to focus on his duty. He’s achieved Nietzsche’s amor fati, a concept that I can’t fathom acquiescing to. He is complacent to his situation. I have become mostly complacent in my current status in life. I’ve avoided getting my driver’s license for about five years, and my job that I hate was only supposed to be for a gap year after high school — I am currently in my fourth year. Complacency is like a gift or skill to Hirayama, whilst it is a curse for me that I struggle to free myself from. Lying down and accepting my current state means not improving. Hirayama has mastered his lot in life, taking the routine by the reins. He has his routine down to a science, and has several locations where those who occupy them know him and have an established connection with him. I have close friends, sure, but not really any third spaces that I have integrated into my schedule. My life doesn’t operate like clockwork as Hirayama’s seems to. Granted, I’m not all bad. Sure, I struggle with productivity (took me FOREVER to write this review), but when it comes to being present and practicing gratitude, I am much better off than I once was. Coming out of an awful headspace in both my tween and teen years, in addition to a borderline mystical experience whilst on edibles, I’ve developed a stronger appreciation for life. I’m also going to school this fall, and am lined up to finally earn my license. I haven’t completely ditched my smartphone, but I bought a flip phone to keep as my main source of communication. My so-called "job that I hate" certainly could be worse. Still, a life like Hirayama’s is one I would not want to live. It looks peaceful, and he’s definitely much less neurotic than I am, but I’ve gained a sense of disgust for menial work. I want to do something meaningful and fulfilling. I tire of consuming slop and being bogged down by my stressful yet tedious job. I want to live well and make cool shit. All in due time, I guess. In the grand scheme of things, Perfect Days’ protagonist is like a background character. Disregarding the philosophical concept that we’re all finite meaningless blobs of flesh (tried to say that less pretentiously than the “floating rock” r/iam14andthisisdeep type shit), Hirayama especially is of little overall importance. He’ll likely leave no legacy, his contribution to society is not nonexistent but also isn’t monumental, and his life does not affect the lives of many others. He is quite inconsequential. He reminded me of my manager, who has told me on multiple occasions that his baseline goal in life is to live as a “background character”. Just be here, do what he can, and die a content man. I think that’s an admirable mindset to have, but the YOLO part of me finds it to be unrewarding. I don’t claim to practice what I preach, as I’m aware I’m often in a rut of passionless inaction, but I like to think my refusal to be totally complacent means that I have hope. There’s something here, I know it. The komorebi, the appreciation for music, the value of human connection, the attention to detail, the maintenance of plant life, and the ethereal quality of dreams. There are several moments that capture the indescribable lustre of life, along with the overwhelming experience of existence that makes you laugh and cry, much like Hirayama. I just found that all of that beauty was lost in the slog of seeing roughly the same thing over and over again with a few unexciting events in between. I was honestly begging for it to end at some point. Watching Perfect Days felt like watching someone else play Tomodachi Life . There’s a few brief glimmers of fun, but a majority of the time all that there is to see is a handful of characters idling around. I liked the scenes that featured 60s-70s music, it reminded me of car rides with my grandpa. The Japanese performance of “House of the Rising Sun” was very captivating. The tic-tac-toe game made me smile. My favourite scene was the shadow tag part, it was so sweet. Unfortunately, a few nuggets of brilliance scattered across a void of plotless dullness do not make an enjoyable film. This review ended up being more of a personal vent than a thorough overview of Perfect Days , but the movie felt so bland that I genuinely didn’t have much more to talk about. I didn’t care for this film on the first go ‘round, but would like to later. Perhaps next time, but not now.

Magnifiques décors et cinématographie. Le film était tristement joyeux et paisible; on suis l’histoire d’un homme qui passe sa vie à nettoyer des toilettes et pourtant, elle n’est pas si ennuyeuse. Sa vie est répétitive , il fait toujours les mêmes activités en boucles ( laver les toilettes, aller au bain public et dormir ) et pourtant il réussi à l’apprécier. Et c’est justement ce que j’ai apprécié dans le film, le fait qu’il suffit juste de prêter attention à ce qui nous entoure pour réaliser la valeur de la vie. Car tout au long du film, le personnage principal fais des rencontres, des expériences, plus ou moins enrichissantes et longues, mais qui laissent toujours une marque dans sa vie. Et tout ce qu’il vis viens un petit temps et repars, en le laissant à sa vie routinière habituelle à la fin,  mais elles viennent, et le comblent de bonheur même pour quelques minutes. Et chaque mauvaise expérience qui va l’affaiblir amène toujours à quelque chose de plus beau. Le personnage ne se contente pas d’exister sans réellement vivre dans l’instant , il remarque chaque détails de son existence , et il est altruiste et humain. très peu de paroles sont dites , parce que ces moments là n’ont pas besoin d’être expliqués et je trouve ça cool. Cependant j’ai mis du temps à vraiment accrocher , et je suis pas trop film très lent, j’aurais quand même aimé qu’il sorte de sa routine et qu’il essaye de garder ou de relancer ce qui est venu dans sa vie, mais je conçois complètement qu’on puisse adorer le film pour les mêmes raisons qui m’ont fait un peu - l’aimer  ; j’aurais aussi aimé qu’il fasse des rencontres qui durent + longtemps et non uniquement des mots échangés de quelques minutes . J’aurais aimé voir des rebondissements, sa routine se déconstruire , mais je sais que ce n’était pas l’objectif du film et je trouve ça bien aussi. Je met seulement 3 ( j’aimerais mettre 3,25 si jpouvais) parce que perso la simplicité c’est pas mon truc, mais j’ai kiffé les messages du film Scène de fin superbe g kiffé J’ai passé un bon moment et le film m’a rendu triste autant qu’il m’a rendu heureuse.

No es para todos y pienso que dentro de esta especie de subgénero de películas "no pasa nada" hay mejores, pero aún así Perfect Days es una película bellísima que cambia tu forma de ver la cotidianidad de la vida, es una historia realmente sencilla, sin grandes giros ni pretenciones solo la vida de un hombre que limpia baños. Una película muy necesaria, muy contraria a lo que lo acelerado de la vida actual nos tiene acostumbrados. Me gusto mucho lo relajante que es ver está película, si bien no es la película más estímulante en cuanto a trama de la historia pues es que eso no es lo que busca daré está obra, entre la excelente dirección, la fotografía que hace que cada momento del film sea bello e incluso el sonido ambiental te transmiten muchísimo esa paz de Hirayama, de apreciar los pequeños detalles. Eso mismo los detalles son un gran acierto de Perfect Days, ver está obra por encima es un gran error, por más que sea una película en la que no pase mucho el verla de fondo es no entender lo que te está tratando de decir, cosas pequeñas como la nota del gato (#) que Hirayama dejaba en el baño, sus fotos, en indígente que siempre veía son las cosas pequeñas y fugaces que hacen en conjunto a Perfect Days una película tan especial sobre ver el mundo sin toda la prisa con lo que lo solemos ver. Un tema que me gustó como fue plasmado fueron lo choque generaciónales entre Hirayama con su sobrina y el wey que lo ayudaba a limpiar, un contraste entre la forma calmada y serena de vivir de alguien que alguien con su experiencia formó contra la forma apresurada y caótica que la juventud y la sociedad actúal tenemos. También me gustaron estás escenas intermedias surrealistas y en blanco y negro entre cada día que la película tiene, como si fueran solo instante de los recuerdos que las rutinas largas nos dan. En fin, este tipo de películas que usan un ritmo lento para resaltar los momentos pequeños siempre son las que más terminan renonando conmigo con el pasar del tiempo y Perfect Days siento que va a ser una de las que más me voy a quedar.

15-20 minutes into the film... what a heartwarming depiction of the joy found in the everyday moments of life. 20-40 minutes into the film... okay what the fuck is wrong with this guy? ~1 hour into the film... one of the most emotionally devastating scenes I can ever remember. Such is Perfect Days, which felt wholly unlike anything I've seen before. Watching this felt like dropping a pebble in a pond or holding a mirror up to a mirror, creating a nesting reflection that stretched to space. Can it be taken at face value? A one-sentence mission statement about the beauty all around us? Or Is there some kind of dark riptide that undermines that beauty? The unspeakable rift that separates a family or the confrontation with mortality; the black and white negatives of the otherwise sun-dappled trees? Or does the contrast of those fissures again underline all the light and goodness we wake up to every morning? Perfect Days is a meditation. Or, maybe It's a haiku - its simplicity and bareness allowing the audience to graft their own meaning upon it. If one test of a writer is to see how much they can communicate with few words, then what Koji Yakusho is doing as an actor in a near silent-film performance is unbelievable. While it must have been difficult to convince studios to greenlight a movie about a janitor in which nothing happens, it's not difficult to latch on to what made this film so moving. Watching it, I felt the same way I do whenever I travel. That when I step away from the interiority of my own life and consider it from a distance I feel as if I am swept up into a greater world around me where anything is possible.

Perfect Days is only my second Wim Wenders film after Paris, Texas , and somehow he’s already given me two incredible films. I honestly feel like I may have peaked way too early with his filmography, because I don’t know how he tops either of these for me. There’s just something so beautiful about the simplicity of this film. Hirayama’s life is incredibly routine and on the surface there isn’t a huge amount happening, but Wenders makes that routine feel meaningful without ever forcing it to be. The pacing is absolutely brilliant. The film is more than happy to sit with Hirayama as he goes about his day, and I never felt bored or impatient. If anything, I found myself becoming more immersed in the rhythm of his life. The sparse dialogue works perfectly with this too. So much of Hirayama’s character is communicated through his expressions, his routines, the people he interacts with, the books he reads and especially the music he listens to. There’s very little need for exposition because the film trusts you to simply observe him and gradually piece together who he is. I also loved the visual style. The colour palette is gorgeous, the editing is really neat, and the Tokyo cityscapes are beautiful throughout. There’s something about the contrast between the busy, overwhelming city and Hirayama’s incredibly simple existence within it that I really loved. Wenders somehow makes cleaning public toilets, eating lunch in a park and driving around Tokyo listening to music feel almost meditative. It’s also interesting comparing this to Paris, Texas. They’re very different films, but there’s definitely a similar fascination with loneliness, human connection and people who have seemingly withdrawn from a previous life. Paris, Texas is much more emotionally heavy and dramatic, whereas Perfect Days feels far more content with simply observing life. It almost feels like Wenders has arrived at a more peaceful understanding of some of the same ideas. And Koji Yakusho is incredible. He does so much with so little dialogue, and the final sequence in particular is such a beautiful example of that. His face says more than pages of dialogue ever could. I think what I loved most is that Perfect Days never feels like it’s trying to convince you that Hirayama’s life is perfect. It’s just showing you that there can be something beautiful in an ordinary life if you actually pay attention to it. The repetition, the routine, the little moments of connection, the music, the trees, the photographs - all of these tiny things gradually become meaningful. This is easily the best thing I’ve seen from Wenders so far, although I’ve only seen two films, so maybe I’ve just started with an unfairly strong pair. Either way, absolutely beautiful from start to finish. 10/10 Top100

A rotina não é uma prisão. É uma prática. Todos os dias Hirayama acorda antes do sol, limpa banheiros públicos em Tóquio, ouve fitas cassete e fotografa árvores. Muitos veem nisso uma vida depressiva, sem ambição. Mas Dias Perfeitos não fala só de rotina. Fala de maneiras de encontrar o infinito no repetitivo. Ele não aspira ser outra coisa. Não há drama, não há "um dia eu vou ser...". Ele simplesmente é. E o filme trata isso como quem reverencia algo grandioso. Simplicidade não significa falta. Significa escolha. Cada gesto de Hirayama é intencional, cada movimento econômico. Não é minimalismo estético. É minimalismo existencial. Hirayama está sempre olhando para cima, capturando a luz filtrada pelas folhas. Isso tem um nome em japonês: komorebi. Não é luz, não é sombra. É o que existe entre elas. Quando ele levanta a câmera, não procura a árvore. Procura outra coisa. Algo que tem a ver com pausa, atenção e a coragem de parar enquanto o mundo corre. [Não por acaso, komorebi é a palavra que dá nome ao meu canal.] Wenders não fez um filme sobre um homem que limpa banheiros. Fez um filme sobre um homem que encontrou paz. E a paz não está em mudar de vida. Está em habitar a vida que a gente tem. Mas o que é, exatamente, um dia perfeito? O filme não responde. Ele mostra. E você? A beautiful film about solitude, routine, melancholy and enjoying the little things. Hirayama’s solitude is beautiful and meaningful, but it may also be a protective shell he has built around himself. Short, sometimes wordless human interactions can be deeply meaningful, yet he has effectively cut himself off from his family for reasons we never fully understand. There is joy in listening to music alone in your car, but also in sharing that music with someone else. He has built a tiny world for himself inside an enormous Tokyo: his apartment, small izakayas and bookshops, the park, the bath house. I loved the way such a vast and sometimes impersonal city becomes intimate through these small spaces, where you encounter the same regulars and gradually become part of one another’s lives. He follows almost exactly the same routine every day, yet every day is slightly different: the light hits the leaves differently and creates new patterns of shadow, the homeless man strikes another absurd pose, a salaryman or a group of children passes through one of the toilets he is cleaning. Routine becomes a way of noticing change rather than escaping from it. A good life can contain both happiness and sadness, tears and a smile at the same time, as in that beautiful final shot.

A slow burner but Wim Wenders explores so many amazing themes throughout the entirety of this film. My favorite, however, is the significance of one’s habitual search for beauty. Although very reserved in his speech, Hirayama, the protagonist, epitomizes this motive. Hirayma, through the eyes of many, lives quite a “dire” life: he’s a toilet cleaner, sleeps on the floor, and showers in a communal bath. Yet, he’s characterized by happiness throughout a large portion of the film because of this habitual appreciation for the little things everyday life offers—the glimmer of sunshine, music on a cassette, or a picturesque view of Tokyo’s architecture. At one point in the film, the bar lady at a restaurant Hirayama is a regular of asks when will things “stay the same,” and I believe this habitual appreciation Hirayama personifies answers that questions. While I do think a consistent routine that brings one joy can be beneficial, I believe having a habitual mindset that nurtures joy is what helps bring true, daily happiness, and which follows something like this: An appreciation of a moment -> a creation of a memory -> the consolidation of that memory While this formula seems to work really efficiently for Hirayama throughout the beginning of the movie, we later on see that this method isn’t bulletproof and other external factors can impede one’s happiness. Ultimately, this film does such an incredible job in demonstrating how happiness is holistic. I could talk so much more about the other themes the film offers or how great Koji Yakusho’s performance was but that’ll be for another time. Really excited to explore more of Wenders’ filmography because the ones I’ve watched so far have been really impressive.

Par quoi commencer ? C’est bien vide. Déjà pour poser les bases. Il ne se passe rien. C’est très contemplatif ce qui ne me dérange pas en général j’aime plutôt bien. Mais il faut une histoire, une trame, quelque chose qui se passe. Là il ne se passe rien, il n’y a pas d’histoire rien. Alors que la base d’un film est de raconter quelque chose, une histoire. On suit juste la vie de quelqu’un, qui ne parle pas en plus, un peu plus de parole aurait peut être aidé à rentrer dans le film. Très surpris de savoir que l’acteur a gagné le prix d’interprétation à Cannes. Sa performance n’est pas magistrale, il ne fait que marcher, faire du vélo, laver et bien sûr ne pas parler. Les images sont belles c’est sur. Mais cela n’est pas grâce à Win Wenders. La ville de Tokyo est photogénique en elle même, il est donc plus aisé d’avoir une jolie photographie. Donc bon pas grand chose à faire pour lui. Sans histoire, sans personnage à qui s’attacher il n’y pas d’émotion, de sentiment. Il y a des tentatives de faire ressentir quelque chose au spectateur mais c’est loupé. On ne peut pas s’attacher au personnage donc on ne ressent rien. C’est donc finalement pas très étonnant que les notes soient aussi hautes. C’est un film pour les bobos de Croix Rousse qui ont besoin qu’on leur dise « la vie est belle » pour s’en rendre compte. Il n’y a pas de message véhiculé non plus. Ça dénonce rien ou ne promeut rien. Donc en globalité c’est vide. Hors film : l’institut Lumière qui surbooke la salle juste pour vendre quelques places en plus et ensuite mettre les gens assis dans les escaliers c’est moche en plus d’être complètement inconscient au niveau de la sécurité. Fin bon c’est à l’image de Thierry Fremeaux le parrain du cinéma français (allez voir l’article de mediapart sur lui c’est très instructif).

O clímax tonal é, entretanto, um plano que converge as atenções para as costas de seu uniforme, onde se lê “limpador de banheiros”. Cinco minutos e PERFECT DAYS já indica que o tio Wenders está com a batuta em riste. Ora, a perspectiva autossuficiente de Hirayama não desapega de uma curiosidade exótica, típica do olhar exterior àquele ambiente. Sua visão de mundo é: 1) formatada por uma idealização do desapego minimalista (o qual, embora suponha valorizar a essência do cotidiano, no fundo, o romantiza); 2) envernizada por um saudosismo nostálgico, doutrinante até, que se acha capaz de "reformar" as novas gerações, sempre tão "distraídas" e "ansiosas". Wenders se nega à possibilidade de alcançar uma concomitância de valores, reforçando os contornos da atualidade para apontar aquilo que defende ou critica. Tanto a cena que, a partir da turista americana, extrai humor dos banheiros japoneses de vidros embaçados, quanto o deslumbre adolescente com a descoberta de Patti Smith são exemplos de um deslocamento espaço-temporal condescendente, firmado na reiteração das diferenças. No ponto de inflexão do protagonista, PERFECT DAYS se desnorteia. Qual seria o contraponto formal deste personagem que sonha em preto-e-branco, fala somente o básico, é praticante da fotografia analógica e se emociona com o balançar das árvores ( i.e. : o Cinema )? Wenders aposta na inserção abrupta de um reels, captado pelo celular de sua sobrinha, personagem tão anacrônica quanto ele. E para sublinhar que as trocas humanas concretizaram alguma transformação, sobrepõe-se a voz de Nina Simone ao alvorecer refletido no rosto de Hirayama. Artimanhas "poetizantes", aparentemente modestas, mas sem o menor efeito real de dissolução ou fusão. A sorte do projeto é que Kôji Yakusho é intérprete delicado o bastante para sustentar uma pataquada dessas com o mínimo de verdade e carisma. Wenders caducou? Não sei, mas tá preguiçoso. O fato do Cinema ser a “expressão de bons sentimentos” (como disse Godard), não significa que é veículo para epifenômenos laboriosamente pré-programados.

In the eyes of Wim Wenders, real poverty or filthy toilets don't exist in Tokyo. There's only aesthetics of life, and that is modesty. Hirayama (Koji Yakusho) is a middle-aged man of few words, who lives in an old apartment by himself. He cleans public toilets in Tokyo during the day, mostly himself but sometimes with a younger co-worker.  After work, he usually has a drink or two at one of his favorite pubs. Other than booze, he finds joy in the simplest things - taking care of plants, literature (Faulkner, Highsmith etc.), music (mainly from 60s-70s, which he listens to on cassette tapes), photography, and a little communication with people.  Although some turn of events reveals he seems to have a complicated past, it doesn't so much as go further than that. Wenders shot the mundane of everyday life in a graceful way it could easily be a commercial for the city. But did it seem like it was filmed by a German director, as Wenders asked the audience at Tokyo International Film Festival? Unfortunately the answer is yes. He even dared to say he discovered that he had Japanese soul, and he always talked about how he wanted to live like the protagonist, according to Yakusho. Just that one statement tells that he doesn’t have a clue what living in Japan is like, or he simply spent too much time away from working class people. Some 30 or 40 years ago, this setting might have worked.  But in 2023?  Take a look at some advertisements for the same kind of jobs as Hirayama’s, and you'll find it pays you max. 10,000 yen per day or 1,200 per hour.  That is merely enough to make a living for one in Tokyo, if you're healthy. And a lot of people are forced to live with such wages. The situation is getting worse and worse in recent years, at least that's what it feels like, that one has to wonder if Perfect Days is a pure satire.  Hirayama may not want much more, but there are tens of thousands of people who have a lot to say to the government which doesn't even pretend to listen to their people anymore.  Instead, the men in Hirayama's life don't seem to care much other than about women (not so much theirs) and the women are either much younger ones who appreciate his sophisticated hobbies and rely on him somewhat emotionally, or an independent woman who heals his soul with her singing (played by a real Enka star Sayuri Ishikawa).  There’s even an adorable boy with Down syndrome who only exists to show that one of the men isn’t as shallow as he seems to be. And the expressive homeless man who magically happens to be played by Min Tanaka, a legendary dancer.  They only show toilets that are designed by acclaimed architects, and none of them even seem occasionally filthy.  If not a satire, it's just a fantasy or fetishization. On top of all this, Wenders lectures us about a Japanese word he seems to find fascinating at the end of the credits.  Needless to say, we know.  And western people love to remind us of beautiful Japanese words.

293. review: Wim Wenders So sorry, but I think that Wim Wenders' new film 'Perfect Days' is one of the biggest disappointments of this year, despite its heartwarming story. It follows the life and barely variable daily routine of a happy, very happy Japanese toilet cleaner in Tokyo. The ageing man begins each day by looking up at the sky and smiling. Then he gets into his car and plays Wenders' favourite retro playlist from a cassette player, shamelessly consuming House of Rising Sun, Lou Reed's Perfect Days and Nina Simone's wonderful Feeling Good in the same film, to the sound of which he drives straight into a brilliant sunrise with the widest, happiest smile on his face in the film's final frames.  He has reason to be happy, because the toilets in this part of Tokyo are extremely varied and hygienic (in the Sibuja district, the protagonist cleans toilets of internationally renowned architects, where guided tours are now being held bc of the film), and he only has to clean two a day, the people are more friendly than not, and although the man's bedroom is bigger than my entire apartment, he still goes to the public bath in the early afternoon, then eats delicious Asian food at a fabulous diner, sits in parks and takes analogue black-and-white photos of people hugging trees and the sunlight streaming through the canopy. In his spare time, he digs up little Japanese maple saplings from the base of large trees and transplants them at home, shaking the soil from their roots as carelessly as possible --- the little seedlings are obviously for bonsai trees --- and in the evenings he reads for hours on the ascetically hard mattress spread out on the floor. The reviews of the film, not only here on lb, are invariably hymns to the joy of simple living. Hard to argue with them. Like Godland or The Lighthouse, this film is a fake: a misappropriation of the Asian, urban version of slow cinema, a saccharine, maudlin, involuntary imitation of the genre. But for those who recognise in the beautiful landscapes of Godland, the superb acting of Lighthouse or the humanist message of Perfect Days something that has strong precedents in their visual memory and that they long for, it's very hard to say that it's all just an illusion, a beautifully photographed lie. Moreover, creators are driven by the same nostalgia when they unconsciously choose imitation over autonomous creation with its own stakes. It's a kind of mimicry. And it is very difficult to call a great director's swan song, intended as a final, happy yes to life, didactic and tasteless. Too bad that Wenders has chosen to convey his message in the most clichéd and unreflective way possible, using the topos of the ideal Asian man, capable of leading a simple and wise life (but listening to Western music!). The protagonist's name is a reference to Ozu's Tokyo Story as a source of inspiration. This is a textbook example of Orientalism, which uses stereotypes to convey a not very complex mental hygienic message (the use of the main motif is revealing, an unconcious slip of tongue the toilet here, but preferably nice and clean toilet, manufactured for the pleasure of global capital, as befits a comfort cinema, the shit of existence is not in the picture, lol). But the point is that you can't just want to make a film about the gift of life, there are some things you can't want or imitate. This should have happened spontaneously, against the gravity of the material --- but this material is concentrated kitsch, one hundred percent kitsch, which has no gravity at all. The particularly poignant result of the film is that, in retrospect, it reveals Wenders' omnipresent tendency towards sentimentality; what once seemed like overflowing emotionality no longer seems so appealing from the perspective of this too-perfect 'Perfect Days'. _____________ Song of the Day: Lou Reed+Bono+Duran Duran+Elton John+David Bowie: Perfect Day www.youtube.com/watch?v=FyYiK8dY_Wk

Excerpted from my second Cannes dispatch for MUBI's Notebook: Less freighted by political portent is Wim Wenders’s Perfect Days, one of the last Competition films to premiere on the Croisette. If attendees were expecting anything like a grand statement, however, the film was surely a disappointment: Perfect Days is most notable for its modest scale, comprising repeated shot sequences that follow the daily routine of an elderly toilet cleaner, Hirayama (played by Kōji Yakusho, who won this year’s Best Actor prize). We watch him as he wakes up, shaves, waters his plants, buys a coffee from a vending machine, gets into his car and drives to work, while each time listening to a different cassette tape (invariably a ’70s or ’80s classic, including, yes, Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day”). During his breaks, we see him take pictures with an old film camera. On the weekends, he drops off a roll of film to get developed, picks up last week’s results, and then methodically sorts through them, selecting the ones he wants to keep and discarding the rest. Like Paterson (2016), Jim Jarmusch’s lyrical, low-key portrait of a bus driver-cum-poet, Perfect Days is fairly direct in its appeal to the quotidian beauty of daily life, and as in that film, the sentiment is a tad pushy and insistent. But Wenders’s dogged commitment to depicting the minutiae of Hirayama’s routine eventually achieves something more than mere preciousness. Across Perfect Days, several encounters take Hirayama away from his routine, involving him in a series of personal dramas of varying interest. The main, or indeed only, operative tension is whether any of them will exert enough force to transform his habitual trajectory. In terms of emotional range, Wenders’s approach is undeniably limited, but his meticulous depiction of Hirayama’s routine pays off in the film’s latter half, where even the smallest deviations in shot selection and composition resonate as strongly as the film’s incipient dramatic turns. In this sense, the film is less a meditation on the fleeting beauty of the everyday than a reflexive exploration of visual and narrative sequencing—an examination of how we use images to mark and measure our works and days.

At what point does personal style become an exercise in moulding an environment to what you would like it to be? Wim Wenders has a distinct style. Laid back, laconic almost. Explorations of people perusing through life, seemingly wanting to find the parts of their surroundings that no one else is looking for. At his best, these can be real investigations of a time and place, such as his early German road movies and at his worst they can be travelogues, like his late-80s documentaries, about off-the-beaten-track subjects which are, when you really look at them, a bit dull. Or certainly seem so when seen through Wenders' occasionally self-interested lens. 'Perfect Days' sits somewhere in the middle of those. This tale of an older Tokyo toilet cleaner, almost hermetically but happily engaging in a routine lifestyle of working, eating, drinking, reading, listening to old cassettes of classic alt-rock and punk is nowhere near as boring as something like 'Notebook on Cities and Clothes'. However, nor is it fully engaging throughout its two hour runtime. As Hirayama, Kōji Yakusho is as engaging as he can be given the restrictions placed on him. When I say that, I can't imagine Wenders as a dictatorial director, giving his actors no say, but the character does feel hemmed in by an in-going decision to have him barely speak. There are several times when that choice feels strained and since he hasn't taken a vow of silence, why not let the man converse a bit more? I don't need a motormouth but something more to help me engage with this character, particularly in the film's difficult middle stretch. This is a complaint central to an overarching enjoyment of Yakusho's performance which is, as has been pointed out elsewhere, very dignified, inviting and graceful but it is indicative of my problem with the film as a whole. There's something missing in the middle. It's like biting down on a chocolate, expecting there to be a sweet centre and finding only air. Like if you combined all the bubbles of an Aero into one and realised how little you're actually getting AND THEN EXPOSE THOSE NESTLÉ BASTARDS! Sorry. Back to the film. So, the middle is missing something. The central stretch feels repetitive rather than revealing more layers, consequently, you start questioning what the film has to say about this foreign world and the answer - honestly - feels like not a lot. Much of that must be lain at Wenders' feet because 'Perfect Days' contains so many tics particular to him, all swept up together, that it feels, as queried at the beginning of this review, like he has crafted a vision of Japan that he'd like to see rather than finding something there. All these quibbles sit amid a feeling of ultimate positivity towards the film. I like Wenders on the whole and I like his worldview, to an extent. Also, honestly, I could complain about him forcing his Western musical tastes onto a Japanese character rather than exploring Japanese music but firstly, that kind of presupposes that Japanese people don't listen to our music and secondly, more importantly, I like that music too. Patti Smith, Lou Reed, Nina Simone, yes please. Plus, the film is so well-meaning and gentle that it's hard to take against it in today's day and age. I even discarded my misgivings that the film was somehow disdainful of the young. Hirayama's young colleague, Takashi, is loud-mouthed and selfish but he is also down and out, needy of cash in an expensive world. Other youngsters in the film come in the form of girls excited by cool music and empathetic to the way Hirayama is treated by society. Wenders has always been forward-looking anyway, as an early adopter of digital filmmaking and I see no judgement of iPhones in his vision. And if the film is mostly surface well, then, what a surface. DP Franz Lustig's 4:3 cinematography, shot on Sony Venice cameras, ties together what conversation there is between the digital and the analogue. Lustig's capturing of Tokyo's forgotten corners brings great luminosity to rain-sodden carparks and even those famously unique Japanese toilets. Intersecting this, charcoal-like, black and white montages briefly intersect the days as possible dreams and memories, beautifully edited together and never interrupting the flow of the film. Writing this now makes me consider that maybe there are other layers I'd missed but I still think there could be more to this film than is ultimately in it. Certainly, the final stretch is the most arresting part of the film, as a couple of encounters with a familiar face and a complete stranger throw Hirayama's equilibrium off and we see much more into who he is, culminating in a elegantly pitched final close-up of Yakusho's face. 'Perfect Days' has many virtues and I like it on the whole but I can't escape the feeling that, if Wenders had put aside some of his preferences, this could have been something much stronger.

Some liken this film to Yasujiro Ozu’s lexicon, but apart from the 4:3 ratio there isn’t all that much in common. The diegetic soundtrack consisting of 1960s and 70s rock music is a bit on the nose, and not at all Ozu-like; a loose narrative that tethers myriad minuscule, but everyday events together to form an ambiguous character study recalls the work of Chantel Akerman. It’s visually alluring and the lead performance is arresting, but like the main character it doesn’t really seem to say much. If it’s a chronology of ambiguously beautiful moments, the film itself winds up feeling ambiguously beautiful.

A handful (although a very big handful) of beautifully honed moments of true serenity, mixed with some less successful reaches towards profundity (and also a comic character that threatens to ruin the whole vibe). The reason for the season is Koji Yakusho, who brings so much pathos and sincerity to this role that it’s undeniable why people connect to this film in any way. Such a special performer, and one sorely needed to bring this down to earth. Did very much enjoy the gently whimsical stuff, just not so convinced by its overall thesis, and it doesn’t always strike a balance between grateful and bitter (although a late scene involving shadows is just, well, perfect). Also disappointed by the music choices, which although fun, seem very much either on the nose or not seeming to dig far enough. Why not dig into the catalog of some of those tapes for the same sounds but less crowd pleasing gimmes? Ironically, the most on the nose drop is I think the most successful, its bittersweet tone enveloping what this film sometimes, and gorgeously, attains, especially in its dream sequences (can’t confirm but I think Wenders’ wife did those? which is lovely). My mom loved it, which was a huge win.

Review courtesy of RMITV’s InReview Leaving the Astor on the last night of MIFF, I eavesdropped on some of the immediate post-showing conversations about Wim Wenders’ new film, Perfect Days. People generally used the correct terms that they would have heard consuming other japanese media, such as “slice-of-life” and “intransitiveness”. Such is the narrative of this movie: we are treated to a relaxingly-paced story about the life of a single and mild-mannered (perhaps reclusive) janitor named Hirayama, as he goes about his public toilet rounds in Shibuya. The narrative is driven mostly by chance encounters with people and family who encourage reflections on mortality, loss and companionship. The film covers all its essential artistic aspects beautifully. Wim Wenders’ admiration for Yazujiro Ozu is consistently evident: throwbacks to Ozu’s textural title cards and his vertical shot composition are two of the most immediate examples that come to mind. You might call this film a “Japanese Arthouse Blockbuster”, if you wanted to illustrate the “Cool Japan” institutional backing of this film: it works with a consortium of not-for-profit and corporate interests to define and beautify Japanese life. The organisation Hirayama works for, The Tokyo Toilet, is a real group that is dedicated to the preservation of some high-profile architectural bathrooms in Shibuya. Hirayama’s uniform has been designed by NIGO (of “A Bathing Ape” fame) and there is ample brand placement from popular food and clothing brands Lawson and Uniqlo. A 2022 press release almost reads as if The Tokyo Toilet is the original inspiration for this film. Family represents the conflicting factor to Hirayama’s modest and emotionally withdrawn life. In reality though, I argue, institutional harms tend to be more of a threat: the forced uprooting of people (such as in the Tsukiji Fish Market for the Olympics), or the mass casualisation of work are more consistent factors of disruption to the ideal Japanese life. This sums up what I don’t like about Perfect Days: such a narrative implies fetishisation for the film festival audience. I cannot ignore the feeling that this film is “awards porn”, aesthetically beautiful, but thematically a bit of a navel-gaze. In this clip from Wenders 1985 documentary Tokyo-Ga, he describes the genius of Ozu’s films is his ability to show life as it truly is. To him, Ozu shows “Long-range truth, lasting from the first image to the last. Films [...] in which the people, the objects, the cities and the countrysides [sic] revealed themselves.” Can truth reveal itself in Perfect Days? Or is it a beautiful simulacrum, contemporary Japan through the gaze of the international film market?

[Cannes23 #28] "The world is filled with many worlds. Some are connected, others are not." Hirayama's life follows a particular routine. He wakes up before dawn, waters his plants, and drives to Shibuya while listening to music — "Pale Blue Eyes", "Redondo Beach", the titular Lou Reed number — to clean public toilets in a park. After work, he heads to an onsen, watches something on television, eats dinner at a bar, and goes to sleep. As he dreams, grayscale mental Polaroids play back the impressions of the day. Sometimes he’s snapped a physical photo of his own to throw in to the mix. It's a simple life, and he loves it. If you haven't clued in yet, this is very much Wim Wenders' PATERSON; though it's hard not to also think of Harry Dean Stanton as I watch his mustachioed protagonist mutely observe the world. He's quiet, bemused, filled with hints of some sadness but — unlike Stanton's wanderer in Paris — it's a sadness he's at peace with, not tamping it down but blurring it into joy. The rhythm of his life plays on for a few days, before other people eventually disrupt it. That's always a hazard, when worlds connect. But frustration, like every other feeling, can be blended in to the melody. Wenders plays it beautifully. Audience response was a bit tepid, but I loved this intentionally quiet, small little movie. It made me nostalgic for the time of my life I spent wandering Tokyo, and it lowered my blood pressure like nothing else at this festival could.

FESTIVAL DE CANNES #35 Wim Wenders, referente del Nuevo Cine Alemán de los años '70 y '80, marcó a varias generaciones cinéfilas, pero desde hacía mucho (demasiado) tiempo que no hacía una muy buena película de ficción (le fue algo mejor con los documentales). Está claro que Perfect Days no alcanzará la importancia en la historia del cine que sí tienen Las alas del deseo o París, Texas, pero significa su regreso a la máxima competencia de Cannes con un film realmente logrado, luego de haber sido seleccionado por “portación de apellido” con engendros como Palermo Shooting. Wenders estuvo desde siempre muy ligado a Japón (Tokyo-Ga es de 1985 y Notebooks on Cities and Clothes, de 1989), así como le ocurrió a tantos otros directores germanos, desde Doris Dörrie hasta Werner Herzog, que también filmaron allí. Y WW lo hace ahora con la historia de Hirayama, un hombre maduro y solitario que se dedica a limpiar los baños públicos de Tokio. No se trata del trabajo más apasionante del planeta, pero él lo hace con esmero, eficacia y dedicación (cabe aclararar que los baños japoneses no son como los nuestros ni los usuarios tan descuidados como en Argentina). Hirayama tiene una rutina que por momentos asemeja Perfect Days a Hechizo del tiempo / Groundhog Day, ya que hace siempre lo mismo: afeitarse, regar las plantas, comprar una gaseosa en una máquina expendedora, iniciar con su camioneta el recorrido por los baños hasta dejarlos inmaculados, ir a una casa de baños, andar en bicicleta, observar con fascinación la torre Skytree, concurrir a los mismos bares y restaurantes, leer un rato a William Faulkner o a Patricia Highsmith y acostarse. Hirayama casi no habla (hasta determinado momentos nos preguntamos si no será mudo) y tiene un patético e irresponsable empleado a su cargo, Takashi (Tokio Emoto), al que le tendrá infinita paciencia. Y después sí surgirán unos (mínimos) conflictos dramáticos con la aparición primero de su sobrina Niko (Arisa Nakano) y luego de su hermana de clase alta Keiko (Yumi Aso). Hirayama es un tipo “analógico”, que parece vivir fuera de época: no sabe qué es un iPhone, escucha clásicos de Lou Reed, The Kinks, Patti Smith, Otis Redding y Van Morrison en cassettes (armé la playlist que comparto aquí debajo), saca fotos en blanco y negro en un parque, revela los rollos y archiva las copias... Sustentada en una precisa puesta en escena sin ostentaciones (recordemos que Wenders es un admirador confeso del estilo austero de Yasujiro Ozu) y en una extraordinaria actuación (minimalista y al mismo llena de matices) de Koji Yakusho, Perfect Days exalta formas sencillas de buscar y encontrar la felicidad. Algunos podrán pensar en conformismo, pero Hirayama conserva incluso con un trabajo que genera reacciones prejuiciosas y despectivas una dignidad, nobleza y bondad infrecuentes en este mundo cínico y violento. El mejor Wenders está de vuelta y es un regreso para celebrar.

Em seu seminal discurso “This is Water” dado aos formandos do Kenyon College em 2009, David Foster Wallace argumentou que devemos abrir os olhos para as belezas da vida comum ao nosso redor. Como um peixe finalmente percebendo a água à sua volta, o escritor de “Graça Infinita” nos convida a perceber o valor inerente às situações mais banais da humanidade. Fazer isso, ele explicou, é uma escolha. Temos participação ativa na decisão de parar e procurar os raios de sol entre as árvores. É fácil traçar paralelos entre a filosofia exposta naquela formatura e o excelente drama corriqueiro Perfect Days, do lendário diretor Wim Wenders. Não acontece nada extraordinário nas duas semanas da vida do Sr. Hirayama (Koji Yakusho) vistas em Perfect Days. Com estilo de vida humilde e idade avançada o suficiente para confundir o Spotify com uma loja, o Sr. Hirayama é um limpador de banheiros públicos em Tóquio com uma rotina tão precisa quanto a execução de seu trabalho. Todo dia, ele acorda com o barulho de uma vizinha varrendo a rua, água suas plantas, compra um café enlatado na maquininha da rua e, sem antes olhar para o céu e sorrir, parte em direção a uma das profissões mais facilmente desrespeitadas e ignoradas da sociedade moderna. Lá, ele transforma a limpeza em sua arte. Entre coletar lixo e tirar manchas de espelhos, este homem de pouquíssimas palavras encontra satisfação. Essa rotina inquebrável inclui, também, uma pausa para o almoço num parque local, onde Hirayama tira fotos para revelar em sua câmera, antiga como as fitas cassetes guardadas em sua velha vã — uma invejável (e valiosa, descobriremos) coleção com hits de The Velvet Underground, Nina Simone e Lou Reed, e outros. Episódios inesperados como a visita de uma sobrinha, a demissão de um subordinado e uma criança perdida podem até mudar seus horários, mas Perfect Days nunca coloca seu protagonista em algo “digno de cinema.” Nessa normalidade, Wenders encontra singelas e silenciosas formas de direcionar nosso olhar para os espetáculos triviais de uma vida bem-vivida. *Essa crítica continua no Chippu*

《Perfect Days》9.5/10 - 「下次是下次，現在是現在」 年度前十確定🥹🥹🥹🥹🥹🥹🥹🥹🥹 怎麼可以拍得這麼好看，用這首歌收尾根本作弊吧，役所廣司如果沒拿影帝我一定討厭魯本一輩子。 Apple Music Soundtrack ⬆️建了一個歌單，但如果你覺得聽歌也算暴雷的話建議不要點 - 木漏れ日(komorebi)，其在日文裡的意義為透過樹梢間的光影交錯，短暫且無法回溯，須臾且具禪意的質地貫穿了整部作品，讓整部電影的調性輕快卻又不失雅性。作為本屆坎城主競賽之作，《Perfect Days》將文溫德斯的思想概念完美地融合在日本文化之中，無論是職人精神抑或是自省的武士道精神都發揮得淋漓盡致，甚至應該說這部作品只有在日本如此具有文化質感的國家才能發揮其敘事的魅力，而我想作為拼接日常意象之作，文溫德斯細膩入微的筆法絕對是賦予了整部作品生命力的最大因素。 在電影一開始便以役所廣司所飾演的中年公廁清潔員的一日作為破題，清楚且自然地將男主內斂且沈穩的個性做了一個很好的展示，而清潔「髒亂」作為男主的工作之一，其呈現的意涵卻又巧妙地與社會對於這份職業的態度全然相反，文溫德斯藉由略為刻意的攝影手法展現社會群體對於這份職業的鄙視與刻板印象，並對比到人內心與外表的「乾淨」與「骯髒」，然而正是這份刻意的佈局造就了後續最大的重頭戲——重逢。 相比許多談及和解與重逢的作品，文溫德斯選擇了一種更為真實的反應去看待男主與其姊姊之間的難解之題，也因此與姪女間的羈絆締結成為了整部電影的最大看點——不能理解母親想法的姪女卻恰恰地能夠理解男主所閱讀的書中人物的孤獨情感，而這個書中的人物又恰恰地是男主本身的人格投影，孤獨的叔姪在一次簡單的談心拾起了他們遺失的情感，那該是多美的時刻。 而唯美的質地呈現電影裡的自然變化更讓這部作品在影像上充滿著溫暖而有力的質感，甚至連角色在雨中騎腳踏車都顯得如此有意義，真的太美了。事實上整部作品也恰恰地能夠反映導演對於komorebi的想法，無論是藉由金錢與卡帶對比有價與無價的方式、在清掃廁所時無意間挖掘的新鮮事物、畏懼打攪姪女而躡手躡腳、被姪女提醒著日常景點的美妙之處……等魔幻的時刻都在逐漸地改變男主的心境——或者說讓他重新地認識、體會到了他自身的「孤獨」。 「孤獨」絕對是這部作品的最大看點，文溫德斯對於生活的體察之細緻在於他的處理方式相比其他過於用力的作品而言是非常自然且不媚俗的，他選擇了逐漸堆砌角色的日常意象去展現這種孤獨。前半段男主習慣了一塵不變的日子與如機械鐘錶般精準的作息，中段藉由轉入與居酒屋老闆的對話去質問「不變」與「萬變」間的優劣時男主開始對自身狀態有所意識，再到後續與姪女的相處和與姊姊的對話，儘管偶爾飄來的雨打亂了男主的心境，電影卻還是藉由了這種漸漸引導的方式去打開男主被包裹起來的內心，讓這種孤獨的意識被慢慢地釋放出來，反倒是拍出了一種有別於純粹「孤獨」的情感，手法非常唯美。 有趣的是整部作品在敘事上的架構幾乎沒有什麼刻意的安排的情節，僅藉由簡單的對話與肢體語言去呈現角色的想法，在電影前一小時男主甚至是沒有超過三句台詞，全然依靠役所廣司的肢體演繹能力，讓人驚艷。而後段男主與姊姊間的談話方式更是完美展現了留白的極致美學，彷彿什麼都說了卻又什麼都沒有說，完美的藉由姊姊的台詞點題，再藉由兩者的距離變化去展現兩個角色間別樣的情感，也因為這種克制的展現更顯得男主在別離之後的情緒釋放之必然與難得。 而在留白的敘事裡，音樂在本片則扮演了至關重要的角色，在與姪女相遇前，本片幾乎每10分鐘便會出現一首輕快且具年代的歌曲（真的要讚嘆文溫德斯的音樂品味，滿滿的good shit），而後段卻完全地失去了音樂的片段，「音樂」在本片所呈現的即是男主認知的內心心靈，這種呈現手法滿有趣的，此外我也很喜歡藉由燈光的變化去強化男主的心情轉變，尤其是最後離開家門時的燈光與清晨灑在他身上的陽光，那種釋然的心態簡直不言而喻。 最後，我想我最喜歡的地方正是文溫德斯寶刀未老的呈現與收斂，河堤邊的兩人以一種詭異卻必然的慰藉將komorebi的意象以實體的方式展現出來，而最後的收尾更是將男主之於整部作品的主體性完美地呈現了出來，尤其以一首經典不敗的老歌來收尾簡直讓整部作品豪無可挑剔之處，我想或許《Perfect Days》正是展現了那種在日本文化內涵裡難以被展現出來的人之情感，我真的太愛太愛這部作品了……

In the world of "Perfect Days," Wim Wenders paints a canvas of life's subtleties, where the routine of protagonist Hirayama (Koji Yakusho) becomes a meditation on the beauty found in everyday moments. Hirayama wakes up and proceeds with a dawn ritual of moustache trimming and plant watering, sets off to start work as a toilet cleaner, a job he approaches with serene satisfaction. He takes a lunch break at a nearby park and comes back home just to repeat is day again and again and again. We see Hirayama’s days pass by in shorter and shorter intervals. Yet he immerses himself in the ordinary with unwavering care. From scrubbing lavatories to capturing black-and-white photographs of trees during lunch breaks, Hirayama's life is a delightful blend of the ordinary and the extraordinary. We get a chance to meander through Tokyo's public restrooms, each a canvas for Hirayama's interactions and reflections, accompanied by a soundtrack featuring classics from Lou Reed, Patti Smith, and the Rolling Stones. The film revels in the monotony of Hirayama's daily life, finding joy in the little things and making peace with the past. It's a slice-of-life that transcends convention, carefully balancing leaning into melancholy with an appreciation for life's subtle moments of beauty. In "Perfect Days," Wenders crafted a cinematic masterpiece that not only captures the essence of a seemingly ordinary life but also invites us to find contentment in the mundane. It offers a mirror to our own existence, bravely confronting the uncomfortable truth of our lack of uniqueness and the inherent meaninglessness of life, which in turn allows for a celebration of life's simplicity. Serving as a reminder that sometimes, the most profound fulfilment arises from cherishing the unassuming joys that make our everyday existence extraordinary like watching trees sway or blasting "The House of the Rising Sun" during the daily commute. "Perfect Days" it's an invitation to savour the beauty of routine, a celebration of the mundane, and a journey into the heart of a man who, with a muted smile and a soulful gaze, takes on the pleasure and pain of a routine life. Wenders direction buoyed by Yakusho's Best Actor-worthy performance create a cinematic gem that resonates with tenderness, humour, and a touch of melancholy, making it a must-see at Cannes 2023.

8am showing, hungover and sleep deprived, wandering into the Lumière , five hours until my flight to Zurich. Just 13 days prior, I was amazed to even be in this theater, but after 10 screenings in this room, and as my viewings began to blend together, I couldn’t help but feel as though I was just checking boxes. And to be frank, the feeling was only exacerbated by the time the 20 minute mark hit, as I watched the routine of a janitorial worker in Tokyo. But then, this film went the exact direction I needed it to go in that moment , at that time. Perfect Days is a testament to honoring individuality for the betterment of oneself. Anyone who knows me well enough will be able to admit: I have always been an individual, not necessarily a loner, but an individual. And here I was at the beginning of a solo excursion across Europe. I couldn’t help but well up at the beauty captured in the small moments. A film about remembering that song you loved in high school and blasting it on a random night, or cooking a nice meal for yourself that's just yours. Working at a job that isn’t necessarily where you imagined yourself because it allows you the means to do what you love on the time off. I’m not sure if any other film I’ve seen has ever reflected my own pathos back to me so directly, or has even been able to portray it so descriptively. I can’t think of a better one to have gone out on with my final day in the Côte d'Azur.

At the risk of being redundant it really does prove that any day can be the perfect day, it’s all a matter of the perspective and the willingness we choose to have. Truly an audiovisual poem and a gift to us all.
